extracted.intended_audience: scholars, translators, and students of Indian literature, comparative religion, and textual criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing, translating, and interpreting Indian poetic and historical works, including identification of authentic texts, qualities of native poetry, and cautions about source reliability and translation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic qualities of Indian poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian poetry often exhibits 'that tender feeling of solitude, and the all-animated world of plants', with 'charming pictures of female truth and constancy' and of 'the beauty and loveliness of infantine nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or emulating Indian verse, look for pervasive tenderness, an anthropomorphic/animistic treatment of nature, emphasis on domestic/infantine beauty, and emotional intimacy rather than Grecian dignified arrangement or rhetorical strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of moral feeling and conscience in Indian verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets style conscience 'the solitary seer in the heart, from whose eye nothing is hid'; sin is represented as incapable of concealment and felt by inanimate elements (sun, moon, fire, air, earth, flood, deep).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect moral transgressions to be depicted as cosmic outrages; evaluate texts for an intense moral sensibility that externalizes conscience in natural elements and uses this for poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of tenderness and terrible imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives of fearful deaths (penitents) or the immolation of widows are 'diversified with many touches of tenderness and feeling' yet remain hard to relish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and preserve the tension between affectionate tenderness and gruesome or tragic imagery when interpreting or translating; the coexistence of both is a feature, not a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sakuntala (Sokuntola) as exemplar: simplicity and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sokuntola 'gives the best idea of Indian poetry' — composition is 'throughout clear and unlaboured', language 'full of a graceful and dignified simplicity', with enjoyment of solitude and reverence for plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Sokuntala as a model: prioritize unforced composition, graceful simplicity, and vivid natural imagery when assessing quality or producing analogous works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrical and dithyrambic qualities (Gita Govinda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gita Govinda is described as 'a series of dithyrambic love songs' with high lyrical beauties that may not survive literal translation; its import can be 'too bold to be susceptible of any literal rendering.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For highly lyrical or erotic devotional pieces, favor approaches that capture tone, rhythm, and emotional force over strict literalness; translators should consider adaptive renderings to preserve lyrical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable/narrative style of Hitopadesha (Hitopadesa)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hitopadesa is 'distinguished by the most artless simplicity and clearness, but interspersed with profound maxims, and many beautiful fragments of the more ancient poems.' It serves as a vehicle for poetic images and moral observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or translating didactic fable collections, preserve the simple narrative clarity while maintaining the embedded maxims and poetic fragments that give them moral and educational force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer translations from original languages (avoid double translations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations executed from modern Hindoo dialects rather than the original language produce 'many blunders and omissions, and not a few barbarous interpolations and additions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always prefer direct translation from the original (Sanskrit, etc.) wherever possible; be highly skeptical of works translated via intermediate modern dialects and note where double translation may have introduced errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess translator fidelity vs. poetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilkins and Jones are 'extremely faithful' translators, yet even faithful literal renderings (Jones's Gita Govinda) can give only 'a faint shadow of the power of the original.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance literal faithfulness with the need to convey the original's poetic effect; note where literal accuracy sacrifices lyrical or rhetorical force and consider measured adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Muslim/Mahometan authors cautiously for Hindu philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mahometan authors can be 'extremely valuable' for eyewitness historical representations (e.g., Ayeen Akbery), but when they treat Hindoo philosophy their criticism is 'childish', translations 'coarse, blundering, and ... unintelligible', and they are 'utterly incapable of feeling or comprehending' opinions so different from their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Muslim-authored histories carefully: accept eyewitness administrative or descriptive material when reliable, but treat their philosophical expositions or translations of Hindu thought with strong caution and cross-check against native sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of authorship/canonical claims by Brahmins
rubrics_metrics.description: The Brahmins 'have a passion for ascribing a fabulous antiquity to all works which in any way relate to their mythology and their system', so study of Hindostan literature requires 'more caution and discrimination' than many fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept claimed antiquity or provenance at face value; investigate internal and external evidence, manuscript history, and possible motives for ascription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect interpolations; avoid dating/authenticity judgments from isolated phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular phrases or sentences may have been 'interpolated by some later hand'; one should be 'very careful not to come to a hasty decision concerning the authenticity or age of whole works' from such fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dating or authenticating texts, rely on broad internal evidence and comparative analysis rather than singular wording or isolated anachronisms; consider the possibility of later insertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess transmission mode and vulnerability to falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian works may have been committed to writing early (sculptured writing exists), reducing some oral-transmission dangers, but they have been 'more exposed to the dangers of wilful falsification and additions.' Puranas contain many suspicious circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether works stem from oral tradition or early writing and evaluate their susceptibility to later falsification; treat Puranas and similar compilatory texts as especially suspect and require corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal integrity as indicator of authenticity (Menu and heroic poems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works (heroic poems, the law-book of Menu) carry 'convincing proofs both of high antiquity and perfect integrity'; these are more to be prized when we 'cannot detect any traces' of additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer texts that show internal consistency, lack of interpolations, and coherent structure as stronger candidates for genuine antiquity and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural sympathy and comparative humility in judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The author warns against judging Indian texts solely by Western standards; many features appear 'repugnant to our ideas', and one 'cannot... be fair judges' of their effects without understanding native spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach Indian works with cultural sensitivity: interpret themes, practices, and aesthetics on their own terms, and avoid imposing foreign evaluative frameworks without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate religious practices/texts by social and intellectual consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian penances and violent austerities 'have an evident tendency to stupify and blunt the mind' and to nurture 'spiritual pride and vanity'; the life of reclusion may deprive society of cultivated intellects unless connected with internal activity benefitting the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing religious texts or practices, consider their practical effects on individual intellect and on social welfare; critique not only doctrine but also institutional consequences.
